subsection.title: The Area Problem
subsection.paragraph: The preceding example touches on the second fundamental problem in calculus: Calculate the area of the region bounded by the graph of a nonnegative function $$f$$ , the $$x$$ -axis, and the vertical lines $$x = a$$ and $$x = b$$ where $$a < b$$ (Figure 7). This area is called the area of the region under the graph of $$\mathbf{f}$$ on the interval $$\lbrack a,b\rbrack$$ or from $$a$$ to $$b$$ .

subsection.title: Defining Area—Two Examples
subsection.paragraph: Just as we used the slopes of secant lines (quantities that we could compute) to help us define the slope of the tangent line to a point on the graph of a function, we now adopt a parallel approach and use the areas of rectangles (quantities that we can compute) to help us define the area under the graph of a function. We begin by looking at a specific example.

subsection.paragraph: Divide the interval $$\lbrack a,b\rbrack$$ into $$n$$ subintervals of equal length $$\Delta x = {(b - a) \slash n}$$ . Next, pick $$n$$ arbitrary points $$x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,\text{and}x_{n}$$ , called representative points, from the first, second, $$\ldots$$ , and $$n$$th subintervals, respectively (Figure 11b). Then, approximating the area $$A$$ of the region $$R$$ by the $$n$$ rectangles of width $$\Delta x$$ and heights $$f\left( x_{1} \right),f\left( x_{2} \right),\ldots,f\left( x_{n} \right)$$ , so that the areas of the rectangles are $$f\left( x_{1} \right)\Delta x,f\left( x_{2} \right)\Delta x,\ldots,f\left( x_{n} \right)\Delta x$$ , we have

paragraph.math: $$A \approx f\left( x_{1} \right)\Delta x + f\left( x_{2} \right)\Delta x + \cdots + f\left( x_{n} \right)\Delta x$$

subsection.paragraph: The sum on the right-hand side of this expression is called a Riemann sum in honor of the German mathematician Bernhard Riemann (1826–1866). Now, as the earlier examples seem to suggest, the Riemann sum will approach a unique number as $$n$$ becomes arbitrarily large.* We define this number to be the area $$A$$ of the region $$R$$ .

subsection.title: The Definite Integral
subsection.paragraph: As we have just seen, the area under the graph of a continuous nonnegative function $$f$$ on an interval $$\lbrack a,b\rbrack$$ is defined by the limit of the Riemann sum

paragraph.math: $$\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left\lbrack {f\left( x_{1} \right)\Delta x + f\left( x_{2} \right)\Delta x + \cdots + f\left( x_{n} \right)\Delta x} \right\rbrack$$

subsection.paragraph: We now turn our attention to the study of limits of Riemann sums involving functions that are not necessarily nonnegative. Such limits arise in many applications of calculus.

For example, the calculation of the distance covered by a body traveling along a straight line involves evaluating a limit of this form. The computation of the total revenue realized by a company over a certain time period, the calculation of the total amount of electricity consumed in a typical home over a $$24$$-hour period, the average concentration of a drug in a body over a certain interval of time, and the volume of a solid—all involve limits of this type.
We begin with the following definition.

note.title: The Definite Integral
note.paragraph: Let $$f$$ be a function defined on $$\lbrack a,b\rbrack$$ . If

The number $$a$$ is called the lower limit of integration , and the number $$b$$ is called the upper limit of integration .

item.paragraph: If $$f$$ is nonnegative, then the limit in Equation (7) is the same as the limit in (6); therefore, the definite integral gives the area under the graph of $$f$$ on $$\lbrack a,b\rbrack$$ .
The limit in Equation (7) is denoted by the integral sign $$\int$$ because, as we will see later, the definite integral and the antiderivative of a function $$f$$ are related.

It is important to realize that the definite integral $$\int_{a}^{b}f(x)\mathit{dx}$$ is a number, whereas the indefinite integral $$\int f(x)\mathit{dx}$$ represents a family of functions (the antiderivatives of $$f$$ ).
If the limit in Equation (7) exists, we say that $$f$$ is integrable on the interval $$\lbrack a,b\rbrack$$ .

subsection.title: When Is a Function Integrable?
subsection.paragraph: The following theorem, which we state without proof, guarantees that a continuous function is integrable.

note.title: Integrability of a Function
note.paragraph: Let $$f$$ be continuous on $$\lbrack a,b\rbrack$$ . Then, $$f$$ is integrable on $$\lbrack a,b\rbrack$$ ; that is, the definite integral $$\int_{a}^{b}f(x)\mathit{dx}$$ exists.

subsection.title: Geometric Interpretation of the Definite Integral
subsection.paragraph: If $$f$$ is nonnegative and integrable on $$\lbrack a,b\rbrack$$ , then we have the following geometric interpretation of the definite integral $$\int_{a}^{b}f(x)\mathit{dx}$$ .

subsection.paragraph: Finally, as promised at the beginning of the section, we will demonstrate that the total daily petroleum consumption of the New England state between 2008 and 2012 was given by the area under the graph of $$f$$ between $$t = 0$$ and $$t = 4$$ .

We begin by dividing the time interval $$\lbrack 0,4\rbrack$$ into $$n$$ subintervals of equal length $$\Delta t = 4 \slash n$$ , with endpoints $$t_{0} = 0,t_{1} = \Delta t,t_{2} = 2\Delta t,\ldots,t_{n} = n\Delta t$$ . In the first subinterval, $$\left\lbrack {t_{0},t_{1}} \right\rbrack$$ , we pick an arbitrary point $$t_{1}^{*}$$ . Observe that because of the continuity of $$f$$ , the values of $$f$$ in $$\left\lbrack {t_{0},t_{1}} \right\rbrack$$ do not vary appreciably from the constant value $$f\left( t_{1}^{*} \right)$$ . So the consumption of petroleum over the period from $$t = 0$$ to $$t = \Delta t$$ is approximately $$f\left( t_{1}^{*} \right)\Delta t$$ million barrels. Similarly, we see that the petroleum consumption over the period from $$t = t_{1}$$ to $$t = t_{2}$$ is approximately $$f\left( t_{2}^{*} \right)\Delta t$$ , where $$t_{2}^{*}$$ is an arbitrary point in the subinterval $$\left\lbrack {t_{1},t_{2}} \right\rbrack$$ . Continuing, we see that the total petroleum consumption over the interval $$\left\lbrack {0,4} \right\rbrack$$ is approximately

paragraph.math: $$f\left( t_{1}^{*} \right)\Delta t + f\left( t_{2}^{*} \right)\Delta t + \cdots + f\left( t_{n}^{*} \right)\Delta t$$

subsection.paragraph: where $$t_{1}^{*}$$ is an arbitrary point in the interval $$\left\lbrack {t_{i - 1},t_{i}} \right\rbrack\left( {1 \leq i \leq n} \right)$$ . Intuitively, we see that as $$n$$ gets larger and larger and the length of each subinterval gets smaller and smaller, the approximation gets better and better. Thus, as $$n$$ becomes arbitrarily large, the sum approaches the limit that we take to be the total petroleum consumption on $$\left\lbrack {0,4} \right\rbrack$$ . But the sum is just the Riemann sum of the nonnegative function on $$\left\lbrack {0,4} \right\rbrack$$ , so its limit gives the area of the graph of $$f$$ under $$\left\lbrack {0,4} \right\rbrack$$ .

Real Estate Figure (a) shows a vacant lot with a $$100$$-ft frontage in a development. To estimate its area, we introduce a coordinate system so that the $$x$$ -axis coincides with the edge of the straight road forming the lower boundary of the property, as shown in Figure (b). Then, thinking of the upper boundary of the property as the graph of a continuous function $$f$$ over the interval $$\left\lbrack {0,100} \right\rbrack$$ , we see that the problem is mathematically equivalent to that of finding the area under the graph of $$f$$ on $$\left\lbrack {0,100} \right\rbrack$$ . To estimate the area of the lot using a Riemann sum, we divide the interval $$\left\lbrack {0,100} \right\rbrack$$ into five equal subintervals of length $$20$$ ft. Then, using surveyor’s equipment, we measure the distance from the midpoint of each of these subintervals to the upper boundary of the property. These measurements give the values of $$f(x)$$ at $$x = 10,30,50,70,\text{and}90$$ . What is the approximate area of the lot?
